label: Implement structured error responses for mcp tools

cards.front: In MCP, what mechanism signals that a tool call failed while still returning a valid, parseable result?
cards.back: The isError flag on the tool result. Setting isError: true tells the model the call did not succeed, but the response is still a structured result — not an uncaught exception.

cards.front: What are the four standard MCP tool error categories and their retryability?
cards.back: validation (No — fix the input), auth (No — escalate to user), not_found (No — verify the identifier), and rate_limit (Yes — wait and retry).

cards.front: What distinguishes a retryable error from a non-retryable one in MCP tools?
cards.back: Non-retryable errors will produce the same failure if retried with the same inputs (validation, auth, not_found); the model should stop and explain. Retryable errors are transient (rate limits, network timeouts) and may succeed on retry after a delay.

cards.front: What metadata hint should you include with a retryable MCP error, and why?
cards.back: Include a retryAfterMs field in the details/metadata giving concrete milliseconds to wait before retrying, so the model has a definite wait target instead of guessing.

cards.front: What fields belong in the structured details object of an MCP error response?
cards.back: field (which input parameter caused a validation failure), resource (the identifier not found), retryAfterMs (ms to wait before retry), and scope (the missing permission scope for auth errors).

cards.front: Why should you never include raw stack traces in MCP error responses?
cards.back: Stack traces leak internal implementation details, are not actionable for a language model, and may expose sensitive path or dependency information to the caller. Sanitize errors before returning them.

cards.front: What consistent envelope pattern should MCP success and error responses follow?
cards.back: Use a consistent shape: always include an error object on failure and always omit it on success. Mixing shapes (e.g., { data: ... } for success but { message: ... } for error) forces the model to guess which it received.

cards.front: What happens if you omit the retryable field on an MCP error, especially a rate-limit error?
cards.back: A missing flag is treated as non-retryable by convention, so rate-limit errors without it cause the model to give up prematurely instead of waiting and retrying.

cards.front: What are the two error-reporting mechanisms in the MCP spec, and which should clients give to the LLM?
cards.back: Protocol Errors (JSON-RPC errors like unknown tool or malformed request) that models are less likely to fix, and Tool Execution Errors (isError: true results with actionable feedback). Clients SHOULD provide tool execution errors to the LLM for self-correction; they MAY provide protocol errors.

cards.front: Why is throwing an unhandled exception a common MCP error-handling mistake?
cards.back: An uncaught throw terminates the tool call with no structured information, leaving the model unable to recover. You should always catch errors and return them as structured isError responses with a specific message.
